title: North America capitals two of five · Central America and Belize
edition: North America capitals · Five regional lessons · John · November 2026
intro: Welcome to the North America capitals, episode two of five. First, I clear the chosen names for a fresh regional lesson.
Seven capitals run down the narrow land between Mexico and Colombia, with Belize on its Caribbean shore.

states.name: Belmopan
lines: Belmopan stands inland in the Cayo district of northern Belize, where the foothills of the Maya Mountains rise behind it.

Built inland after Hurricane Hattie wrecked Belize City in 1961, it is one of the smallest capitals in the world: only a few tens of thousands of people live there, and its National Assembly building was designed to look like a Maya temple.
Remember Belmopan as the hurricane-proof capital, rebuilt inland and shaped like a Maya temple.

states.name: Guatemala City
lines: Guatemala City lies in a highland valley at about 1,500 metres, on the chain of volcanoes that runs through Guatemala.
The capital moved here after earthquakes destroyed Antigua Guatemala in 1773, and it is the largest city in Central America.
Remember Guatemala City as the capital that replaced a ruined Antigua, and the largest city in Central America.
states.transition: Let's bring Guatemala City into view.

states.name: Tegucigalpa
lines: Tegucigalpa lies in a valley of the Honduran highlands, on the Choluteca river, in the centre of the country.
A name from Nahuatl whose meaning is disputed; it shares its role as capital with Comayagüela, across the river, and its airport, Toncontín, is known as one of the hardest in the world to land at.
Remember Tegucigalpa as the two-city capital, with Comayagüela across the river and the world's hardest landing at Toncontín.

states.name: San Salvador
lines: San Salvador lies in the Valley of the Hammocks, below the San Salvador volcano, on the Pacific side of El Salvador.
Rebuilt many times after earthquakes, it lost its archbishop Óscar Romero, who was shot while saying Mass in 1980 and was made a saint in 2018.
Remember San Salvador as the city in the Valley of the Hammocks, rebuilt after earthquakes and the home of Saint Óscar Romero.
states.transition: Let's bring San Salvador into view.

states.name: Managua
lines: Managua lies on the southern shore of Lake Managua, in the lowlands of central Nicaragua.
Made the capital in 1852 as a compromise between the rival cities of León and Granada; an earthquake in 1972 destroyed its centre.
Remember Managua as the compromise capital, chosen to settle the old rivalry between León and Granada.

states.name: San José
lines: San José lies in the central valley of Costa Rica, between the mountains and the Pacific, at about 1,170 metres above the sea.
The capital since 1823, in 1884 it was among the first cities in the world with electric street lighting, and its National Theatre, of 1897, was paid for by a tax on coffee exports.
Remember San José as the coffee-tax theatre of 1897, and one of the first cities on earth lit by electricity.
states.transition: Let's bring San José into view.

states.name: Panama City
lines: Panama City stands on the Pacific side of the isthmus, where the canal cuts through the narrow land between the two oceans.

Founded in 1519, the first European city on the Pacific coast of the Americas; the pirate Henry Morgan sacked the old city in 1671, and it was rebuilt a few kilometres away. It is often said to be the only capital with a rainforest inside its limits.
Remember Panama City as the first Pacific city of the Americas, rebuilt after Henry Morgan's sack, with rainforest inside its limits.
states.transition: Let's bring Panama City into view.

recap: Belmopan and Guatemala City sit in the north of the isthmus, Tegucigalpa, San Salvador and Managua in the middle, and San José and Panama City at the narrow southern end.

Remember the hurricane-proof capital shaped like a Maya temple, the capital that replaced a ruined Antigua, the two-city capital with Comayagüela, the Valley of the Hammocks, the compromise between León and Granada, the coffee-tax theatre and the first Pacific city of the Americas.
